briefs.title: Typesense query field coverage testing
briefs.description: Use Typesense query field coverage testing to prove name, description, and author are searchable while taxonomy and slug remain filter fields.
briefs.coreQuestion: How do you prove name, description, and author are searchable while slug and taxonomy fields remain filter-only?

outline.heading: What Must Typesense Query Field Coverage Testing Prove?
outline.coverage: Define searchable fields from query_by and separate them from fields used only for filtering, faceting, sorting, or result mapping.

outline.heading: How Do You Build a Typesense query_by Contract Test?
outline.coverage: Index unique tokens in name, description, author, slug, and taxonomy fields, then query each token with production parameters.

outline.heading: What Does Search Author Field Testing Verify?
outline.coverage: Prove an author-only token finds the document and remains compatible with author facet filtering.

outline.heading: Slug Not Searchable Regression Cases
outline.coverage: Assert a token present only in slug does not match unless it is also present in one of the three query_by fields.

outline.heading: How Do Searchable Versus Faceted Fields Differ?
outline.coverage: Map query_by, filter_by, and facet_by behavior and test taxonomy arrays through filters rather than free-text assumptions.

outline.heading: Typesense Field Coverage Matrix
outline.coverage: Cover each collection field and label its query, filter, facet, sort, and response roles.

outline.heading: Field Token, Query Parameters, and Expected Hits
outline.coverage: Present one unique token per field with expected found counts and facet output.

outline.heading: How Do You Run the Field Coverage Procedure?
outline.coverage: Create a disposable collection, index controlled documents, execute production search options, and assert positive and negative cases.

outline.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
outline.coverage: Answer questions about query_by, facets, slug discovery, author search, array fields, wildcard queries, and relevance.

outline.heading: Conclusion
outline.coverage: Summarize the field-role contract and point to search-focused QA skills.

procedurePlan.heading: How to verify Typesense field coverage
steps: Create documents with a distinct token in each candidate field.
Run searchSkills with one token at a time.
Assert name, description, and author tokens return the intended document.
Assert slug-only and taxonomy-only tokens do not match free-text search.
Apply taxonomy filters and verify those same fields work as facets.
Snapshot the production query_by and facet_by parameter strings.

codeExamples.title: Capture production query and facet fields
codeExamples.focus: Assert query_by and facet_by include exactly the intended fields.

codeExamples.title: Index one-token-per-field documents
codeExamples.focus: Build fixtures that conform to skillsSchema and isolate every field role.

briefs.cta: Browse search testing skills at /skills and apply the field coverage matrix to your index.

briefs.title: Typesense connection timeout testing
briefs.description: Use Typesense connection timeout testing to verify the five-second client limit and distinguish search outages from an unconfigured service.
briefs.coreQuestion: How do you test the five-second Typesense connection timeout and distinguish timeout failures from an unconfigured client?

outline.heading: What Must Typesense Connection Timeout Testing Distinguish?
outline.coverage: Separate missing configuration, refused connection, stalled connection, remote error, and successful slow response outcomes.

outline.heading: How Do You Write a Typesense Timeout Error Test?
outline.coverage: Point the client at a controlled server that accepts but delays a response and measure rejection near the configured limit with tolerance.

outline.heading: What Does Search Node Unavailable Testing Cover?
outline.coverage: Compare DNS failure, connection refusal, stalled socket, and server error without assuming they share one exception shape.

outline.heading: Typesense Client Retry Behavior
outline.coverage: Observe the installed client behavior using one configured node and avoid claims about retries not proven by the source or official client.

outline.heading: How Do You Assert the Five Second Connection Timeout?
outline.coverage: Use monotonic timing, bounded tolerance, and fake or local delayed transport so CI scheduling does not create fragile exact-time assertions.

outline.heading: Configured Search Outage Test Versus No Configuration
outline.coverage: Assert getTypesenseClient returns null without an API key, while a configured remote failure rejects from searchSkills because no local catch exists.

outline.heading: Configuration and Failure Outcome Matrix
outline.coverage: Present client state, network behavior, elapsed range, searchSkills result or error, and endpoint impact.

outline.heading: How Do You Run a Deterministic Timeout Procedure?
outline.coverage: Reset the singleton, isolate environment variables, use a delayed test server, call searchSkills, and assert time plus error handling.

outline.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
outline.coverage: Answer questions about connection versus request timeouts, retries, singleton reset, missing API keys, CI tolerance, and fallback behavior.

outline.heading: Conclusion
outline.coverage: State the two distinct service states and direct readers to search reliability skills.

tablePlan.title: Typesense client state and outage matrix

procedurePlan.heading: How to test the Typesense timeout
steps: Save and isolate all Typesense environment variables.
Verify a missing API key returns the empty unconfigured result.
Start a local HTTP server that accepts the request but delays its response.
Configure the singleton to use that server and call searchSkills.
Measure elapsed time with a monotonic clock and assert a bounded timeout window.
Restore environment state and close the delayed server.

codeExamples.title: Configure a five-second Typesense client
codeExamples.focus: Exercise singleton creation, missing-key behavior, one-node configuration, and connectionTimeoutSeconds.

codeExamples.title: Observe configured and unconfigured search outcomes
codeExamples.focus: Assert empty fallback only for a null client and rejection for a configured remote failure.

briefs.cta: Browse search reliability skills at /skills and add a controlled timeout server to your tests.

briefs.title: leaderboard top fifty boundary testing
briefs.description: Use leaderboard top fifty boundary testing to verify inclusion, exclusion, ranking, and tie behavior at positions 50 and 51 for every filter.
briefs.coreQuestion: How do you test inclusion, exclusion, and tie behavior at positions 50 and 51 for every leaderboard filter?

outline.heading: What Must Leaderboard Top Fifty Boundary Testing Prove?
outline.coverage: Define the 50-row contract for all, trending, hot, and new, plus rank assignment after truncation.

outline.heading: How Do You Build a Top 50 Ranking Cutoff Test?
outline.coverage: Seed at least 52 controlled skills and assign sortable values that make positions 49 through 52 unambiguous.

outline.heading: What Proves Leaderboard Position 51 Exclusion?
outline.coverage: Assert the expected boundary ID is absent, the list has exactly 50 rows, and returned ranks end at 50.

outline.heading: SQL Limit Tie Boundary Cases
outline.coverage: Place equal primary sort values across positions 50 and 51 to expose missing or incomplete tiebreakers in each filter.

outline.heading: How Does Ranking Cutoff Fixture Design Work?
outline.coverage: Control installCount, weeklyInstalls, qualityScore, createdAt, and the hot formula independently while retaining deterministic IDs.

outline.heading: Leaderboard Maximum Rows Contract
outline.coverage: Test fewer than, exactly, and more than 50 available rows and verify no client parameter changes the hard route limit.

outline.heading: Filter, Boundary Values, and Expected IDs
outline.coverage: Present a table for all four filters with sort formula, boundary fixture, included ID, excluded ID, and residual tie risk.

outline.heading: How Do You Run the Top-50 Procedure?
outline.coverage: Seed, clear each cache key, request each filter, and assert length, rank sequence, position 50, and exclusion of position 51.

outline.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
outline.coverage: Answer questions about SQL LIMIT, ties, rank gaps, cache keys, hot scoring, fewer rows, and pagination alternatives.

outline.heading: Conclusion
outline.coverage: Restate the boundary contract and point readers to leaderboard automation skills.

procedurePlan.heading: How to verify the top-50 boundary
steps: Seed 52 skills with controlled values for every ranking field.
Compute expected order for one filter in the test fixture.
Clear that filter's leaderboard cache key.
Request the filter and assert exactly 50 rows and ranks one through 50.
Assert the expected boundary ID is last and position 51 is absent.
Repeat the calculation and assertions for all, trending, hot, and new.

codeExamples.title: Exercise every limit-50 branch
codeExamples.focus: Verify each filter truncates before rank assignment and preserves its sorting contract.

codeExamples.title: Seed controlled ranking values
codeExamples.focus: Create 52 rows with explicit install, weekly, quality, and timestamp values.

briefs.cta: Open /leaderboard and use testing skills from /skills to automate every cutoff branch.

briefs.title: category response grouping contract testing
briefs.description: Use category response grouping contract testing to verify four stable arrays, correct row placement, and explicit empty groups in every response.
briefs.coreQuestion: How do you prove every category lands in the correct testingType, framework, language, or domain array and empty groups remain present?

outline.heading: What Must Category Response Grouping Contract Testing Prove?
outline.coverage: Define four always-present array keys, recognized type-to-key mapping, row preservation, and no cross-group duplication.

outline.heading: How Do You Write a Category API Group Shape Test?
outline.coverage: Validate the top-level JSON keys and array types before checking row-level content.

outline.heading: What Is the Empty Taxonomy Group Contract?
outline.coverage: Seed no rows for one or more recognized types and prove their keys remain present with empty arrays.

outline.heading: TestingType Framework Language Domain Mapping
outline.coverage: Map each stored type exactly to its response key and verify names, slugs, metadata, and IDs remain unchanged.

outline.heading: How Do You Build a Category Grouping Integration Test?
outline.coverage: Use a real database fixture and cache reset so selection, grouping, serialization, and response behavior are tested together.

outline.heading: Stable Category Response Keys
outline.coverage: Assert exact key presence independent of row counts while avoiding brittle assumptions about array order not promised by the query.

outline.heading: Stored Type and Response Group Matrix
outline.coverage: Present the four valid values, destination keys, empty-group behavior, and representative row assertions.

outline.heading: How Do You Run the Grouping Procedure?
outline.coverage: Seed one row per recognized type, clear cache, request categories, assert shape and membership, then rerun with an empty group.

outline.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
outline.coverage: Answer questions about empty arrays, key naming, row order, cache reset, unsupported types, and schema validation.

outline.heading: Conclusion
outline.coverage: Summarize the stable response contract and link to the categories and skills pages.

tablePlan.title: Category type to response group contract

procedurePlan.heading: How to verify category response grouping
steps: Seed one uniquely identifiable row for each recognized category type.
Delete the categories:all cache key.
Call GET and assert the exact four top-level array keys.
Assert every seeded ID appears once in its expected group only.
Delete all rows for one type and clear cache again.
Assert the corresponding key remains present as an empty array.

codeExamples.title: Assert four initialized response groups
codeExamples.focus: Verify group keys, row placement, empty arrays, and cached response serialization.

codeExamples.title: Seed one row per stored category type
codeExamples.focus: Create deterministic fixtures with unique IDs, slugs, and type values.

briefs.cta: Open /categories, browse related QA skills at /skills, and automate the four-group contract.

briefs.title: Drizzle sort alias contract testing
briefs.description: Use Drizzle sort alias contract testing to prove each public sort value selects the expected column and unknown values fall back to trending.
briefs.coreQuestion: How do you prove every public sort alias maps to the expected Drizzle order and unknown values use trending?

outline.heading: What Must Drizzle Sort Alias Contract Testing Prove?
outline.coverage: Define the accepted sort strings, shared aliases, descending columns, deterministic ID tiebreaker, and trending fallback.

outline.heading: How Do You Test the API Sort Parameter Contract?
outline.coverage: Issue requests for newest, quality, highest_quality, popular, most_installed, trending, missing, and unknown values.

outline.heading: What Is a Drizzle Order By Mapping Test?
outline.coverage: Use fixtures whose createdAt, qualityScore, installCount, and weeklyInstalls produce visibly different orders.

outline.heading: Unknown Sort Fallback Testing
outline.coverage: Assert unrecognized and case-variant values select weeklyInstalls descending, then ID descending for ties.

outline.heading: How Do You Build a Popular Alias Regression Test?
outline.coverage: Prove popular and most_installed return the same ordered IDs for a stable fixture.

outline.heading: Highest Quality Sort API Aliases
outline.coverage: Compare quality and highest_quality and verify both use qualityScore rather than install metrics.

outline.heading: Sort Value, Column, Alias, and Fallback Matrix
outline.coverage: Present every public input with expected primary order, equivalent alias, tie key, and response example.

outline.heading: How Do You Run the Sort Contract Procedure?
outline.coverage: Seed conflicting metric orders, call each alias, assert ID sequences, and include missing plus unknown controls.

outline.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
outline.coverage: Answer questions about descending order, aliases, unknown values, tie handling, pagination, case sensitivity, and defaults.

outline.heading: Conclusion
outline.coverage: Summarize the public-to-database mapping and point to the sortable skills directory.

procedurePlan.heading: How to verify sort aliases
steps: Seed skills whose four sortable fields each imply a different order.
Request every documented sort value with a fixed page and limit.
Assert the returned ID sequence for each primary column.
Compare popular with most_installed and quality with highest_quality.
Request a missing and an unknown sort value.
Assert both fallback cases match the trending order and ID tiebreaker.

codeExamples.title: Table-test the route sort switch
codeExamples.focus: Exercise every alias, default branch, descending order, and unique ID tiebreaker.

codeExamples.title: Seed contradictory sort metrics
codeExamples.focus: Create rows that expose any accidental mapping to the wrong field.

briefs.cta: Open /skills, exercise every sort alias, and use the related QA skills to keep the contract stable.
